title: The Fourteenth Floor

jokes.text: Warm-up guy tells audience the sign says 'applause' after pretending it says something else
jokes.setup: Warm-up guy starts reading aloud then backtracks — 'No, no. L... I'm kidding.'
jokes.punchline: The sign literally says 'applause' — he was pretending the audience had a choice.
jokes.explanation: A standard warm-up bit that works as background texture — cynical meta-commentary on manufactured audience enthusiasm. Functional but not particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This will come as very good news to my grandmother who needs a spotter to pick up a spoon.

jokes.text: The announcer intro credits Larry as wearing new pants he can't wait to show off as the reason for the show
jokes.setup: Standard late-night show announcer intro building excitement for the host
jokes.punchline: The reason given for Larry's entrance is that he's wearing new pants he can't wait to show off — trivially vain and petty
jokes.explanation: The joke subverts the grandiose announcer intro format by replacing a dignified reason for Larry's entrance with naked vanity about new pants. It's efficient character comedy — Larry as vain peacock established before he even walks out — and the contrast with the bombastic 'Lar-r-r-y-y-y Sanders!' delivery makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: listen, when you live in the bay area, it's not easy to say 'bay area man.'

jokes.text: "You're so much better than last night's crowd."
jokes.setup: Larry thanks the audience for their applause in the conventional warm way
jokes.punchline: He immediately insults the previous night's audience, revealing his competitive pettiness even toward anonymous crowds
jokes.explanation: A tight, economical gag that reads as both on-air performance and genuine Larry Sanders character truth. The insult to the previous crowd reveals Larry's insecurity and competitive nature in a single offhand line. The casualness of delivery is what sells it.

dialogue.line: The intoxicated man later tried to convince police he was one of those new, crazy, flesh-eating viruses.

jokes.text: "This will come as very good news to my grandmother who needs a spotter to pick up a spoon."
jokes.setup: Study shows elderly people benefit from weight lifting three times a week
jokes.punchline: Larry's grandmother is so frail she needs a spotter to lift a spoon
jokes.explanation: Solid late-night monologue joke — the spoon detail is specific and visual enough to be genuinely funny. Escalates a reasonable premise (elderly weight lifting) to an absurd but logical extreme. Could be from any host, so low on character integration, but structurally clean.

dialogue.line: When asked to comment on this, a white house aide said, 'please go away. If she finds out I talked to you, she'll hurt me.'

jokes.text: "Listen, when you live in the bay area, it's not easy to say 'bay area man.'"
jokes.setup: Larry stumbles on his words reading 'bay area man' from the teleprompter
jokes.punchline: Rather than acknowledging he simply stumbled, he offers a meta-commentary that turns the flub into an implicit joke about the phrasing itself
jokes.explanation: A nice self-aware recovery that works on two levels: as Larry saving face in real time, and as a meta-joke about the sounds of 'bay area.' The rewatch bonus comes from understanding this is in-character performance mode — Larry papering over a teleprompter stumble with false profundity.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: 'you know, you're too old, you can't see, and you're a woman,' which, by coincidence, is exactly the same excuse Bill Clinton used to get out.

jokes.text: "The intoxicated man later tried to convince police he was one of those new, crazy, flesh-eating viruses."
jokes.setup: A man has been charged with biting an exotic dancer on her left buttock
jokes.punchline: His defense is that he is a flesh-eating virus
jokes.explanation: The punchline has a nicely absurdist logic — using a topical 1990s news panic (flesh-eating viruses) as an alibi for a biting incident. The specificity of 'left buttock' and 'flesh-eating virus' creates a satisfying escalation. Generic late-night but above average in its absurdist pivot.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It's about a father and his 5 wacky kids. It's about a father and 4 kids. It doesn't even add up to 6, and yet it's called... the 6 of us. They're too cheap to hire the sixth guy.

jokes.text: "Please go away. If she finds out I talked to you, she'll hurt me."
jokes.setup: Poll says most people believe Hillary Clinton has too much power; a White House aide is asked to comment
jokes.punchline: The aide is terrified of Hillary and begs the reporter to leave before she finds out
jokes.explanation: Standard mid-90s Hillary-as-scary-powerful-woman joke. The cowardly aide voice is a clean device but the premise was already a cliché at the time. Functional monologue filler.

dialogue.line: They said, 'well, that's... hopefully, people watch every week to wonder who the other one is.'

jokes.text: Hillary tried to join the Marines but was told she was too old, couldn't see, and was a woman — "which, by coincidence, is exactly the same excuse Bill Clinton used to get out."
jokes.setup: Hillary Clinton was rejected from the Marines for three reasons when she was 27
jokes.punchline: The exact same criteria Bill Clinton used to dodge the draft — the misdirection being that we expect a Hillary punchline but get a Bill one, and that the excuses don't map cleanly onto Bill
jokes.explanation: One of the stronger monologue jokes. The structure is excellent — three setup conditions that seem built for a Hillary punchline, then the tag pivots to Bill in a way that's both unexpected and politically pointed. The absurdity of 'too old, can't see, you're a woman' mapping onto Bill Clinton's draft situation gives it an extra layer. Clean misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I actually believe that you could replace all of our network executives with chimps and, other than the, uh, hygiene factor going up, why, no one would know the difference.

jokes.text: Larry's on-air rant about the network show 'The 6 of Us' which only has 5 characters
jokes.setup: Larry describes a new network show called 'The 6 of Us' about a father and his kids
jokes.punchline: The math doesn't work out — it only adds up to 5 — and the network's response is that viewers will tune in weekly wondering who the sixth person is
jokes.explanation: This is pure Larry Sanders DNA — insider showbiz contempt for network stupidity, delivered as a monologue bleed into backstage reality. The joke about the network spinning the math error as a creative hook ('people tune in to wonder who the other one is') is sharp and specific. The 'Idiots.' button is perfect. Strong character integration because this is Larry doing what he does — performing contempt — but the line between on-air and off-air is deliberately blurry.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Great show, great guests tomorrow, you go home, have a glass of wine, whack off. I'll see you tomorrow.

jokes.text: Artie's phone call mid-show — 'I can't meet with you right now. I'm right in the middle of a show... Well, if it's a problem, I'll meet you right here at my monitor, right on the floor.'
jokes.setup: Artie receives a call from the network while the show is actively taping
jokes.punchline: Rather than setting a proper time, Artie casually offers to meet the caller right there at his floor monitor during the show — absurd improvised professionalism
jokes.explanation: Classic Artie — unflappable, pragmatic to the point of absurdity. The offer to hold a meeting at his monitor during the taping captures his character perfectly: the show is everything, but Artie will deal with anything without losing his cool. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Dr. Don! I didn't recognize you with my pants on!

jokes.text: "I actually believe that you could replace all of our network executives with chimps and, other than the hygiene factor going up, why, no one would know the difference."
jokes.setup: Larry is continuing his on-air bit about network stupidity
jokes.punchline: The chimps would be an improvement — specifically because chimps have better hygiene than network executives
jokes.explanation: The inversion is well-executed — the joke expects the hygiene punchline to land against the chimps, then pivots to say chimps would be cleaner. The 'other than the hygiene factor going up' phrasing is crisp. A bit familiar as executive-bashing but the specific execution is sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: If you stand up too fast, you'll get hit in the head by the boom.

jokes.text: "Nothing to talk about, nothing to critique. Great show, great guests tomorrow, you go home, have a glass of wine, whack off. I'll see you tomorrow."
jokes.setup: Larry asks Artie if it was a good show post-taping, expecting a real post-mortem
jokes.punchline: Artie's entire post-show note is to go home, drink, and masturbate — the escalation from wine to 'whack off' is the gag
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Rip Torn's Artie delivering 'go home, have a glass of wine, whack off' as a completely matter-of-fact post-show debrief is pitch-perfect character comedy. The escalation from wine (refined) to masturbation (crude) lands because it's so casually delivered — Artie treating both as equally practical advice. Enormously quotable, deeply in character. Larry's stunned 'That's the post-show critique?' caps it perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: His heart's in the right place, but he keeps his brain in a box at home.

jokes.text: Larry mistakes Dr. Donaldson (the vitamin B shot doctor) for Daniel Palmer from the network
jokes.setup: Larry expects Daniel Palmer from the network to appear; a man shows up
jokes.punchline: The man is actually the doctor who gives Larry vitamin B shots — identity mistaken
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the vitamin B payoff that follows. The misdirection is clean but the joke is more of a connector than a standalone comedic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I gave him some candy and a balloon and sent him on his merry way.

jokes.text: "Dr. Don! I didn't recognize you with my pants on!"
jokes.setup: Larry realizes the man is Dr. Donaldson, who gives him vitamin B shots
jokes.punchline: The inversion of 'I didn't recognize you with your clothes on' — Larry is usually the one with pants off for the shots
jokes.explanation: A neat inversion of the classic 'didn't recognize you with clothes on' joke, flipped so that Larry is the one usually undressed. It's economical, unexpected in context, and reveals something embarrassing about Larry's routine in a single offhand line. The 'Ha ha!' that follows suggests Larry is quite pleased with himself, which adds a layer.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Or maybe we say that you've discovered the network family tree and you pull out this dead little Bush or somethin'.

jokes.text: Artie says 'I was expecting something different' upon seeing the young network liaison Daniel Palmer
jokes.setup: The network has sent a liaison to discuss Larry's on-air remarks
jokes.punchline: Artie's barely concealed disappointment/surprise at Palmer's youth — 'I was expecting something different' — is a masterclass in understatement
jokes.explanation: Pure Rip Torn. The line is ostensibly polite but devastating — Artie is clearly unimpressed and barely hiding it. The comedy comes from what's NOT said. 'I was expecting something different' communicates contempt more efficiently than any insult. High character integration because only Artie would deliver this with that particular patrician disappointment.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I believe that's the same message on, uh, Michael Jackson's answering machine.

jokes.text: Palmer: 'I'm network liaison for late-night programming.' Artie: 'I was expecting Melanie or Dennis. No. No. No, this isn't a big enough issue for either Melanie or Dennis to get involved.'
jokes.setup: Artie learns Palmer's title
jokes.punchline: Artie names specific people he expected (more senior), and Palmer's response inadvertently diminishes the very issue Palmer was sent to address — it's not important enough for the real executives
jokes.explanation: The joke works on an industry-insider level — Artie's hierarchy knowledge signals his veteran status, while Palmer's clarification that this 'isn't a big enough issue' for senior executives undercuts his own authority. Clever, dry, and true to network politics.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Not always easy for the network to find the chair.

jokes.text: Hank barges in looking for his keys, is introduced to Daniel Palmer, and asks if Palmer is connected to the 'Circus of the Stars' special
jokes.setup: Artie is in a serious meeting with a network liaison about Larry's on-air jokes
jokes.punchline: Hank hijacks the meeting to advance his own agenda — getting onto Circus of the Stars — completely oblivious to the actual stakes
jokes.explanation: A great Hank moment. The Circus of the Stars desire is perfectly petty and self-serving — Hank cannot read a room, and his pivot from sketch complaint to celebrity circus inquiry in a single breath is deeply funny. The 'Very good' when Palmer says he's not connected to it is a nice button — Hank treating Palmer's irrelevance to his personal agenda as a positive.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel Palmer
dialogue.line: Well, I was in nursery school.

jokes.text: Artie to Hank: 'If you stand up too fast, you'll get hit in the head by the boom.'
jokes.setup: Hank says he's 'a little steamed' about something.
jokes.punchline: Artie assumes Hank's complaint is the boom mic hitting him (apparently a recurring thing) — not anything substantive.
jokes.explanation: A gem of character-specific comedy. The implication is that Artie has warned Hank about this before — it's a running problem specific to Hank's obliviousness. The joke works because it tells us everything about how Artie views Hank: as someone who causes small, predictable, avoidable disasters.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, so you write as well?

jokes.text: Hank asks Daniel Palmer if he's connected to the 'Circus of the Stars' special, seemingly relieved when the answer is no.
jokes.setup: Hank has just barged into a serious meeting.
jokes.punchline: His priority is not the network controversy but whether this guy can get him on Circus of the Stars — and he leaves satisfied with the answer.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Hank: he interrupts a potentially career-altering meeting to check on a circus variety show. The relief in 'That's very good' is priceless — Hank's priorities are consistently, hilariously inverted from what any normal person would care about.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel Palmer
dialogue.line: Well, I only know what's on until 8:30 because that's my bedtime.

jokes.text: "You'll have to excuse Hank. His heart's in the right place, but he keeps his brain in a box at home."
jokes.setup: Hank has just left the room after an embarrassing non-sequitur about Circus of the Stars
jokes.punchline: Artie's perfectly calibrated explanation — the brain-in-a-box line — is both a real insult and delivered with the warmth of genuine fondness
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's strongest individual line. The phrasing is genuinely original — 'keeps his brain in a box at home' is a fresh spin on the 'heart in the right place' idiom, inverting its warmth into a precise put-down. It's devastating and affectionate simultaneously, which is exactly who Artie is. Highly quotable, perfectly economical, couldn't come from anyone but Artie. Comfortably an 8+ joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Manson had a family.

jokes.text: Phil enters saying 'The sun is shining. The grass is green. All's well in Hollywood. Unless you're working with Shannen Doherty.'
jokes.setup: Phil offers an idyllically positive Hollywood greeting
jokes.punchline: The exception is Shannen Doherty — the mid-90s byword for difficult TV personality
jokes.explanation: The structure is a classic false-positive setup with a dark exception. The Shannen Doherty reference was very topical in 1994 and lands as an industry in-joke. Slightly cheap because it's a pure celebrity name-drop, but the contrast with the sunny opening is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Fine. I'll write it up. Have it upstairs by the end of the day.

jokes.text: Larry and Artie get distracted playing Tetris on a Game Boy in the middle of their serious conversation
jokes.setup: Artie and Larry are having a serious strategic conversation about the network meeting
jokes.punchline: Both are immediately seduced by Tetris — 'Addictive, isn't it?' 'Yes, it is very addictive.' — the game derailing adult professional conversation
jokes.explanation: A nice visual/behavioral joke — two adults who should be strategizing are completely captured by a handheld video game. Works because it deflates the professional seriousness of the scene and is very true to the period. The shared 'addictive, isn't it' exchange gives it a warm absurdist quality.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Fine. I'll write it up. Have it upstairs by the end of the day.

jokes.text: Larry's idea: 'Maybe we say that you've discovered the network family tree and you pull out this dead little Bush or something.'
jokes.setup: They're brainstorming a desk piece mocking the network's 'we're a family' rhetoric
jokes.punchline: The 'dead little Bush' is a visual/wordplay gag — the Bush family connection and the double meaning of a dead shrub representing the network family tree
jokes.explanation: The 'dead little Bush' is a clever idea in the writers' room sense — it's a visual/political pun — but it's pitched as a concept rather than executed as a joke, so the comedic impact is diffuse. Earns credit for the cleverness of the conceiving but the delivery is loose.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: The network respects you too much to play that kind of game.

jokes.text: Larry's on-air non sequitur about the circus — 'Boy, do I love the circus' — out of nowhere during the show
jokes.setup: The show is rolling, Larry and Hank are doing their between-guest banter
jokes.punchline: Larry randomly declares love for the circus apropos of nothing, leaving Hank visibly confused ('Pardon?')
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is structural — the audience can see Larry's mind is clearly on the Circus of the Stars conversation, causing him to blurt out 'I love the circus' mid-show. The fact that the real-life Hank storyline is bleeding into the on-air persona is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I've been makin' waves since the midwife tugged me out of my mother's underside.

jokes.text: "I believe that's the same message on Michael Jackson's answering machine."
jokes.setup: Larry describes the ringmaster calling out 'boys and girls, children of all ages'
jokes.punchline: That's Michael Jackson's answering machine message — a child predation implication
jokes.explanation: A dark-subversive joke that was edgy in 1994 (the first Jackson accusations were 1993). The structure is clean — a straight line about a circus call followed by the celebrity redirect — but the premise was already being done by many comics at this time. Functional shock joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: we'll kick 'em in the ass.

jokes.text: Larry brings Daniel Palmer from the network onto the show as a 'goodwill ambassador' for an on-air apology segment
jokes.setup: The network wants an on-air apology from Larry for his anti-network jokes
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'apology' is to publicly humiliate the network's representative on his own show — the opposite of an apology
jokes.explanation: The entire segment is a sustained ironic joke — the apology tour becomes an ambush. Bringing the network's own representative onto the show to be ridiculed in front of a live audience is a characteristically Larry Sanders move: passive-aggressive, cowardly-brave, and ultimately self-defeating. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Who the fuck do you think I am, Mr. Chips?

jokes.text: "Not always easy for the network to find the chair." (after Palmer awkwardly searches for his seat)
jokes.setup: Network liaison Daniel Palmer sits down on the show — the logistics of finding the guest chair visibly take a moment
jokes.punchline: Larry editorializes dryly — the network can't even manage to find a chair
jokes.explanation: A quick, mean needle disguised as helpfulness. The chair fumble becomes a metaphor for network incompetence. Larry is clearly enjoying himself and the audience can feel it — he's weaponizing politeness.

dialogue.line: If only the arabs and israelis would give cup-a-soup.

jokes.text: Palmer reveals he was VP of comedy development at NBC before his current job — implying he was demoted to nursery school, then back up
jokes.setup: Larry asks what Palmer did before the network job since 1987; Palmer says 'I was in nursery school' — expecting a joke — then Larry asks 'And before that?'
jokes.punchline: Palmer reveals he was VP of comedy development at NBC — so the timeline goes: VP at NBC, then nursery school, now network liaison. The career trajectory is absurdly backwards
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully structured misdirect. The 'I was in nursery school' line seems like the punchline — it's funny on its own as a comment on Palmer's youth. Then Larry's follow-up 'And before that?' milks an extra beat, and the real punchline (VP at NBC) lands because the career reversal — big executive job, then school — is the actual absurdity. A two-stage misdirection that rewards the setup. One of the episode's best structured jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, God! Aiyeee!

jokes.text: 'By any chance, have you seen the new show The 6 of Us?' / 'Um, only the episodes I wrote.'
jokes.setup: Larry brings up the show he mocked the night before — baiting Danny
jokes.punchline: Danny reveals he wrote episodes of the show Larry called idiotic — a perfectly deadpan self-implication
jokes.explanation: A beautiful callback payoff. Larry set up The 6 of Us as a punchline to end all punchlines, and now the network's representative turns out to have written it. The economy is excellent — 'only the episodes I wrote' does all the work in six words. Strong character callback that deepens the satire.

dialogue.line: I get a bad tooth, he goes to Maui.

jokes.text: Artie's phone call from the network mid-show, cheerfully telling them Marisa Tomei is coming up and she's 'so lovely' before deferring the conversation
jokes.setup: The network is clearly calling to complain during the live taping
jokes.punchline: Artie deflects by talking up Marisa Tomei's loveliness as if that's the most important thing — his casual dismissal of the network's complaint mid-show
jokes.explanation: Artie's management of the network during the show is consistently funny — he handles them like a cranky parent handles a child, with charming dismissiveness. The Marisa Tomei non-sequitur is a delightful deflection.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Get off my ass. I'm hungry.

jokes.text: "Well, I only know what's on until 8:30 because that's my bedtime."
jokes.setup: Larry asks Palmer about the network's fall lineup
jokes.punchline: Palmer can only speak to the early schedule because 8:30 is his bedtime — a joke about his youth that pivots back to the kid premise
jokes.explanation: A callback to the nursery school joke, extending the running gag about Palmer's absurd youth. The 8:30 bedtime is a specific, funny detail and the delivery presumably gets a big in-studio reaction. Economical and well-integrated into the on-air interview structure.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I heard he's found the lord.

jokes.text: "Does anyone at the network stay up past 8:30?"
jokes.setup: Palmer's 8:30 bedtime joke
jokes.punchline: Larry extends it by implying the entire network operates on children's bedtimes — meta-commentary on network executives' cultural cluelessness about late-night
jokes.explanation: Larry milks the bedtime joke with a sharp follow-up that doubles as genuine industry commentary — network executives who oversee late night TV don't actually watch it. It's a well-timed callback that adds satirical dimension.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: If I was 10 years on that boat, I'd find the lord, too.

jokes.text: Artie's 'Manson had a family' response to the network's 'we're a family' speech
jokes.setup: The network executives are giving the standard 'we're a family' corporate reassurance speech
jokes.punchline: Artie: 'Don't give me the family crap. Manson had a family.'
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke, and one of the best lines in the show's run. The setup is a corporate cliché ('we're a family') that everyone in the room has heard a thousand times. Artie's rebuttal — 'Manson had a family' — is perfectly calibrated: two words that devastatingly reframe the family metaphor as a threat rather than warmth. It's quotable, original, character-perfect (only Artie could say this with that authority), and structurally impeccable. The brevity is the genius. Reaches the calibration threshold of the Snip-snap anchor in its category.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Gavin mccloud doesn't know one fucking ring from another.

jokes.text: "No offense, Melanie. That's a delightful hair Bob. Is that what you call the style?"
jokes.setup: Artie has just said 'tit for tat' in a heated argument about network scheduling; Melanie is presumably present
jokes.punchline: Artie pivots to complimenting Melanie's haircut mid-argument — simultaneously apologizing for the inadvertent wordplay and disarming the room with false sweetness
jokes.explanation: A very funny Artie moment — the accidental 'tit for tat' leading to an overly gracious redirect about Melanie's hair is exactly the kind of comedy the show does best. Artie acknowledges the potential offense with excessive, theatrical gallantry, which is funnier than any apology would be. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I already had my... lunch. I had a ham and bourbon sammich.

jokes.text: Artie offers to write up the apology himself, then discovers the network wants it from Larry, on air — double reveal
jokes.setup: Network wants an apology; Artie offers to draft it himself
jokes.punchline: First escalation: they want it from Larry. Artie again offers to write it. Second escalation: they want it on air. Artie immediately accepts, fully reversing his previous position
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is very well-executed — each new demand is met by Artie's identical offer to 'write it up,' until the on-air demand forces him to agree too quickly. The speed of his capitulation at 'And they shall get it. We're a family.' — co-opting the very phrase he just destroyed with the Manson line — is a perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Is this the ham talking?

jokes.text: Artie tells Larry the network meeting was 'standard stuff' and denies any mention of an apology — then reveals it in stages
jokes.setup: Larry asks what the network said; Artie downplays it completely
jokes.punchline: The truth comes out in escalating stages: 'not a thing' → 'there was something mentioned in passing' → 'the network might want an apology' — Artie managing Larry's anxiety by rationing the bad news
jokes.explanation: A recurring comic structure in the episode — Artie lying to Larry's face and then immediately retracting. This version has the best escalation: the denial is fullest, the reveal most staged. It's procedural comedy about information management, and it's very much an Artie specialty.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The little guy with the palsy, right?

jokes.text: Larry: 'Apologize to those bastards after they made me go on national television and say I had a drug problem? Pricks! Prick bastards!' Artie: 'That, too.'
jokes.setup: Larry explodes about the apology demand, bringing up a past grievance about being forced to publicly admit a drug problem
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'That, too' — acknowledging Larry's additional grievance with minimal effort — is perfectly timed to deflate Larry's rage
jokes.explanation: Two words — 'That, too' — that do enormous work. Larry's explosion is passionate and specific (the drug problem admission is a real grievance); Artie validating it as an afterthought, barely engaged, is perfectly timed. It's Rip Torn's absolute peak mode: the minimum possible words for the maximum comedy. Justifies 8+ by its economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I hope you like it short and uneven.

jokes.text: Larry accuses Artie of being 'afraid of making waves at the network'; Artie responds: 'I've been making waves since the midwife tugged me out of my mother's underside.'
jokes.setup: Larry challenges Artie's courage, accusing him of backing down from the network
jokes.punchline: Artie's retort is a boast so viscerally specific ('my mother's underside') that it becomes its own kind of comedy — proudly vulgar, unexpectedly vivid, impossible to argue with
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'my mother's underside' is doing all the work. It's sufficiently gross and clinical that it becomes funny on phonetics alone, but it's also a perfect character assertion — Artie's rebelliousness is as old as birth itself. The image of the midwife moment as the beginning of a lifetime of wave-making is absurdly grandiose and completely in character. One of Rip Torn's best lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No. I'm the goat. They're gonna fire me, see? They say that I can't handle you, so they're gonna bring in their own man.

jokes.text: "We'll lay it at their feet, and when they bend over to pick it up, we'll kick 'em in the ass."
jokes.setup: Artie and Larry are planning the on-air apology strategy
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'apology' is actually a Trojan Horse — they'll offer it sincerely enough that the network bends over, then physically kick them. The metaphor is both strategic and somehow literal in Artie's world.
jokes.explanation: A memorable Artie line — the folksy violence of 'kick 'em in the ass' as a literal plan is funny because Artie sounds like he means it physically. The bending-over-to-pick-something-up setup is a clean piece of physical comedy logic. Very quotable, strongly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Before we get any further into tonight's show, I would like to say that... we've been doing some joking about the network the last couple of weeks, and that is my responsibility. I take full responsibility for it, and if I so overstepped my boundaries and insulted the network in any way, I apologize, and I would like to be a member of the network family again...

jokes.text: Larry: 'Unless you think he's doing his homework.' Artie: 'Who the fuck do you think I am, Mr. Chips?'
jokes.setup: They're trying to book the young network exec back for the on-air apology bit; Larry jokes about the kid doing homework
jokes.punchline: Artie's furious 'Who the fuck do you think I am, Mr. Chips?' — the obscure reference to the gentle schoolmaster from the 1939 film — is perfectly incongruous with Artie's roughness
jokes.explanation: The Mr. Chips reference is characteristically Artie — a gruff man who reads, who has seen everything, who casually invokes a 1930s film character as the measure of how gentle he is NOT. The 'Who the fuck do you think I am' delivery paired with that specific reference is a character comedy peak. Larry's 'OK. Sorry. Good-bye, Mr. Chips.' button extends it perfectly. Justifies 8+ through the specificity and character-perfect incongruity.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: that nice lady is gonna be, uh, tripping over a little thing called a subpoena.

jokes.text: Larry asks 'Who the fuck do you think I am, Mr. Chips?' when Artie makes a homework joke, Artie replies 'OK. Sorry. Good-bye, Mr. Chips.' / 'Ta-ta.' / 'Ta-ta, Mr. Chips.'
jokes.setup: Larry is exasperated by the homework joke
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately adopts 'Mr. Chips' as a new nickname and repeats it with warm farewell — the joke now becomes a brief running gag within the scene
jokes.explanation: The 'Mr. Chips' bit works because Artie immediately weaponizes Larry's exasperated reference. The back-and-forth 'Ta-ta, Mr. Chips' is an endearing button on a tense scene. Good comic rhythm between Shandling and Torn.

jokes.text: Hank's on-air segment: presenting a bouquet and 'Lipton Cup-a-Soup' to the network as a peace offering
jokes.setup: Larry sends Hank to the 14th floor to present a peace offering to the network
jokes.punchline: The offering is flowers and Cup-a-Soup — a comically inadequate, cheap, and random gift for a corporate diplomatic gesture
jokes.explanation: Cup-a-Soup as a diplomatic peace offering is inspired. It's so specifically wrong — not flowers AND something nice, but flowers AND the laziest possible pantry item — that it reads as a perfect Hank choice. The absurdity deepens with the assortment discussion ('clearly proves we've come in peace').

jokes.text: "If only the Arabs and Israelis would give Cup-a-Soup."
jokes.setup: Hank is about to present Cup-a-Soup as a peace offering to the network
jokes.punchline: Larry extends the metaphor to the Middle East peace process — as if Cup-a-Soup is the missing ingredient in geopolitical diplomacy
jokes.explanation: A terrific callback that elevates the Cup-a-Soup bit by applying its absurd logic to a larger geopolitical stage. The deadpan is perfect — Larry says this as if it's a genuine observation. Short, punchy, quotable.

jokes.text: Larry on air: 'is that an assortment of cup-a-soup, or is that just one kind?' / 'It's an assortment, which I think clearly proves we've come in peace.'
jokes.setup: Hank is live at the network with his cup-a-soup peace offering.
jokes.punchline: Larry and Hank earnestly debate whether the assortment proves their peaceful intentions — treating the cup-a-soup as a diplomatic signal.
jokes.explanation: The assortment debate is a perfect piece of absurdist commitment comedy — both characters treating this completely seriously. 'Which I think clearly proves we've come in peace' is the line of the sequence: Hank has internally developed a whole logic around soup variety as diplomatic signaling. Highly quotable, great rewatch value.

jokes.text: The receptionist tells Hank she can't let him through without a name or extension number
jokes.setup: Hank has arrived at the network offices to present the apology peace offering to 'anyone at the network'
jokes.punchline: The network's own receptionist won't let Hank see anyone without a specific name or extension — the peace mission is being stymied by bureaucracy
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe setup — the elaborate apology mission is already failing at the front desk. Works as buildup to the physical comedy that follows. Hank's obliviousness and persistence are the engine here.

jokes.text: Larry's off-mic 'Blow by her, Hank' — coaching Hank to barrel past the receptionist
jokes.setup: Hank is being blocked by the receptionist
jokes.punchline: Larry, watching from the studio, casually instructs Hank to 'blow by her' as if it's a totally reasonable diplomatic strategy
jokes.explanation: Larry directing Hank like a football coach directing a running back — 'blow by her' — in the context of a peace mission is funny because it's simultaneously the worst and most Larry-like advice possible. The casualness of it is perfect.

jokes.text: Hank trips over a cable, falls, and injures his ankle — live on television during the peace mission broadcast
jokes.setup: Hank is attempting to barge past the receptionist with his bouquet and Cup-a-Soup
jokes.punchline: He trips over a cable, crashes, and the whole mission devolves into chaos as Hank screams 'Please don't touch my ankle!'
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of Hank's spectacular fall during a live peace mission is well-earned. The escalation from bureaucratic obstruction to physical injury to live TV disaster is the show at its best. 'Please don't touch my ankle!' becomes a memorable panic line. Impact is high because this is the most energetic physical moment of the episode.

jokes.text: Larry's increasingly panicked on-air handling of Hank's fall: 'Hank? Hank? Did his earpiece fall out? Hank. Don't...please don't touch my ankle! ...Let's cut. Let's come back. His earpiece has fallen out. We'll apologize to the network another...another time.'
jokes.setup: Hank has fallen and appears injured during the live apology broadcast
jokes.punchline: Larry's priority is not Hank's wellbeing but the show — the apology is abandoned with 'We'll apologize to the network another time' as if it's just a scheduling inconvenience
jokes.explanation: Larry's total inability to focus on Hank's actual injury because he's worried about the broadcast reveals his character perfectly — self-centered, show-obsessed. The moment where he clearly repeats Hank's 'don't touch my ankle' from the earpiece is funny, and the cheerful 'We'll apologize another time' dismisses Hank's crisis as a logistics problem.

jokes.text: Hank trips over the cable, falls, and screams 'Oh, God! Aiyeee!' on live television
jokes.setup: Hank attempts to bypass the receptionist.
jokes.punchline: He immediately trips over a cable and falls — the 'goodwill mission' ends in physical catastrophe on live television.
jokes.explanation: A great physical payoff to the whole sequence. The escalation from 'diplomatic mission' to 'man falls on live TV' is satisfying, and the show plays it for maximum awkwardness with Larry scrambling to cut away.

jokes.text: Larry on air: 'His earpiece has fallen out. We'll... we'll apologize to the network another... another time.'
jokes.setup: Hank has fallen and is screaming in pain on live television.
jokes.punchline: Larry coolly attributes the failure to a technical malfunction (earpiece) and kicks the apology down the road.
jokes.explanation: Larry's composure while Hank possibly lies injured on the network floor is peak Larry Sanders: the show comes first, the cover story is issued instantly, and the apology is efficiently vaporized. 'Another time' is a perfect evasion.

jokes.text: Hank confronts Larry after the sketch: 'This is what happens when you screw around with the network. Innocent victims get caught in the crossfire.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just injured his ankle during the live apology stunt and lost the Circus of the Stars ringmaster job
jokes.punchline: Hank frames himself as an 'innocent victim caught in crossfire' — the language of war reporters applied to losing a celebrity circus gig
jokes.explanation: Hank's sense of victimhood is always outsized, but the specific grandiosity of 'innocent victims in the crossfire' for a celebrity circus opportunity is a nice comic beat. It captures his self-pity and self-importance simultaneously.

jokes.text: Artie to staff: 'I don't need a bunch of butt-licking pencil-pushing pissants pissing my day away! Now get the hell upstairs before I introduce the point of my boot to your collective asses! Get!'
jokes.setup: Artie has been calmly managing the situation, then suddenly erupts at his staff
jokes.punchline: The alliterative explosion — 'butt-licking pencil-pushing pissants pissing' — combined with the boot threat is an Artie eruption in full flower
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn's eruption scenes are the show's closest thing to crowd-pleasing physical comedy. The alliterative string of P-words is almost musical — 'butt-licking pencil-pushing pissants pissing' — and the 'point of my boot to your collective asses' threat feels genuinely credible coming from Artie. High character integration and quotability; the kind of line fans of the show quote.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Good looking prosthetic.' Hank: 'Not the foot. The circus of the stars.'
jokes.setup: Artie sees Hank hobbling after the ankle injury
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'good looking prosthetic' implies he thinks Hank lost the foot; Hank clarifies he meant the Circus of the Stars gig — the actual loss is the celebrity circus
jokes.explanation: A beautifully compressed exchange. Artie's casually observational 'good looking prosthetic' about Hank's apparent limb loss, followed by Hank's clarification that the real loss is the circus gig, is a wonderful piece of double misdirection. The comedy rests on Hank treating the celebrity circus as a greater loss than a hypothetical foot. Perfect economy, strong character integration for both. One of the episode's best quick exchanges.

jokes.text: 'They're going with Gavin McLeod.' / 'I heard he's found the Lord.' / 'Oh, who hasn't? If I was 10 years on that boat, I'd find the Lord, too.'
jokes.setup: Hank is furious that Gavin McLeod (Captain Stubing from The Love Boat) got the Circus of the Stars ringmaster job instead of him
jokes.punchline: Artie's observation that McLeod 'found the Lord' is met with Hank's explanation — ten years on a TV boat would make anyone find religion
jokes.explanation: The Love Boat theology joke is a gem — the logic of being trapped on a TV cruise ship for ten years leading to religious conversion is funny because it's almost reasonable. The industry-insider texture (Gavin McLeod, Circus of the Stars) makes it feel lived-in and specific.

jokes.text: 'I heard he's found the Lord.' / 'Oh, who hasn't? If I was 10 years on that boat, I'd find the Lord, too.'
jokes.setup: Hank is furious that Gavin MacLeod (Captain of The Love Boat) got the Circus of the Stars ringmaster role over him.
jokes.punchline: Artie's logic: finding religion after 10 years on a cruise ship is entirely understandable — almost a geographical inevitability.
jokes.explanation: A sharp insider joke with perfect internal logic: Artie sympathizes with Gavin MacLeod's spiritual journey by noting the conditions. The implication that The Love Boat would drive anyone to God is mean-spirited celebrity comedy with a genuinely funny kernel of truth.

jokes.text: "Gavin McLeod doesn't know one fucking ring from another."
jokes.setup: Hank is furious about losing the ringmaster job to Gavin McLeod
jokes.punchline: Hank's technical critique of McLeod's ringmastery — 'doesn't know one fucking ring from another' — implies that Hank himself is a circus expert
jokes.explanation: The line works because Hank's expertise in ring-knowledge is entirely self-assigned — he's clearly never been a ringmaster either. The specificity of 'one fucking ring from another' as a criterion of fitness is perfectly petty Hank. High quotability and character integration.

jokes.text: Hank reveals the network offered him a consolation prize: being shot out of a cannon by Barbara Eden
jokes.setup: After losing the ringmaster job to Gavin McLeod, Hank describes the network's offer
jokes.punchline: The offer is: being shot out of a cannon by 'Jeannie' (Barbara Eden from I Dream of Jeannie) — a deeply specific, deeply ridiculous celebrity circus act
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'shot out of a cannon by Barbara Eden' is genuinely funny — it conjures a very clear, very ridiculous image. The 'Jeannie?' clarification adds a beat of appreciation for the absurdity. Pure mid-90s showbiz surrealism.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I hope you turned them down.' Hank: 'Of course, I plan to. But just in case, are we on hiatus the week of the 23rd?'
jokes.setup: Larry expresses hope that Hank turned down the cannon offer
jokes.punchline: Hank says he 'plans to' but immediately checks Larry's schedule to keep the option open — he hasn't turned it down at all
jokes.explanation: The 'of course, I plan to' followed by immediate schedule-checking is a perfect Hank moment — his dignity and his desperation for celebrity attention are in constant war. The 'just in case' is doing beautiful work. Strong character integration, very funny structure.

jokes.text: Hank reveals Larry has already taken Hank's prescription painkillers: 'Yes, but I checked with Beverly. You already have the ones they gave me.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Hank got painkillers for his ankle injury
jokes.punchline: Beverly already confirmed Larry has Hank's prescription — Larry preemptively took Hank's medication
jokes.explanation: Devastating character joke. Larry — who earlier had to go on TV and admit a drug problem — has apparently already taken the painkillers meant for Hank's ankle injury. The callback to the drug problem (referenced earlier in the episode) gives it extra resonance. 'I checked with Beverly' confirms this was systematic, not accidental. Very dark, highly in character, and enormously funny in context.

jokes.text: Artie's 'ham and bourbon sammich' lunch
jokes.setup: Larry arrives for their lunch meeting and asks if they're eating in or going out
jokes.punchline: Artie has already had his lunch — a 'ham and bourbon sammich,' which he describes contentedly while clearly a bit drunk
jokes.explanation: The 'ham and bourbon sammich' is a perfect Artie detail — specific, slightly alarming, completely in character for a man of his generation and appetites. The word 'sammich' is doing work too — it's informal and fond, suggesting this is a beloved meal. High character integration; only Artie Sanders would call this lunch.

jokes.text: Artie's speech: 'You've been biting the hand that feeds you and the hand's gonna come right up and smack you right upside the head.' Larry: 'Is this the ham talking?'
jokes.setup: Artie gives Larry a stern lecture about antagonizing the network
jokes.punchline: Larry deflects Artie's serious speech by suggesting it's the bourbon ham sandwich talking
jokes.explanation: A clean callback to the bourbon sandwich, using it to undercut Artie's authority in a way that's affectionate rather than mean. Larry's delivery of 'Is this the ham talking?' is the kind of deadpan that deflates pomposity perfectly. The callback structure works well.

jokes.text: Artie reveals the network's punishment: replacing Larry's stylist Kristoff with 'Ernie, the guy that does the guys in the news department — the little guy with the palsy.'
jokes.setup: Artie warns Larry there will be budget cuts if he doesn't apologize
jokes.punchline: The specific punishment is replacing his upscale stylist with a man described as 'the little guy with the palsy' — implying Larry will have short, uneven haircuts
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the punishment is funny — not budget cuts, not losing a guest, but losing his STYLIST to a man with palsy. The character detail reveals how important appearance is to Larry and how precisely the network has calibrated the punishment. Slightly uncomfortable with the palsy reference but delivered as character judgment, not mockery of disability.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I hope you like it short and uneven.' / 'Well, I'm certainly not going to apologize under some threat. What are they going to do, fire me?'
jokes.setup: Artie has just described the palsy-haircut consequence; Larry defies the threat
jokes.punchline: Artie then reveals the real threat: they'll fire ARTIE, not Larry, installing their own man to monitor him
jokes.explanation: The escalation from hair stylist to Artie's job is well-structured. Larry's bravado ('what are they going to do, fire me?') is immediately deflated by the revelation that his leverage comes at Artie's expense. The emotional stakes suddenly become real, which gives the comedy more weight.

jokes.text: Artie: 'He's gonna stand right next to that monitor glaring at you with his ear wired to the 14th floor.'
jokes.setup: Artie explains what happens if he's fired: the network will place their own man on the floor
jokes.punchline: The image of a network drone standing next to the monitor, ear wired to the 14th floor, glaring — is a vivid surveillance-state comedy image
jokes.explanation: The image is funny because it's paranoid but totally plausible in this world — the network panopticon made flesh. 'Ear wired to the 14th floor' is a vivid and funny specific detail. The comedy is in the absurd corporate surveillance imagery.

jokes.text: Larry's on-air apology: solemn, personal, seemingly sincere — structured as a real apology with full accountability
jokes.setup: Larry walks out and appears to deliver a genuine, heartfelt apology to the network
jokes.punchline: The entire apology is immediately revealed to be a bit — Artie's plan fully executed, the sincerity weaponized
jokes.explanation: The Artie plan pays off — the apology is sincere-seeming enough that the network is pleased, but we know it's a trap. The comedy is in the dramatic irony: we've been told what's coming, and watching Larry perform sincerity is funny because we know it's cynical. Strong callback to Artie's 'kick 'em in the ass' strategy.

jokes.text: Artie taking Melanie's congratulatory call: 'It was a magnificent apology, wouldn't you say?' — then relaying: 'It was meant to be a joke.'
jokes.setup: The apology has apparently pleased the network; Artie receives a call from Melanie praising it
jokes.punchline: Artie's flat relay to us that it 'was meant to be a joke' while performing gracious acceptance to Melanie — playing both sides simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Artie managing Melanie's praise while revealing the con to us in the same breath is the show's double-consciousness at its best. The flat 'it was meant to be a joke' to the viewer while being effusively warm on the phone is a perfect piece of character comedy.

jokes.text: Hank's post-fall interview: 'That nice lady is gonna be tripping over a little thing called a subpoena.'
jokes.setup: Artie tells Hank the network lady tripped over a cord — it wasn't her fault
jokes.punchline: Hank is threatening to sue the network lady who fell over a cord — framing a mutual accident as something she did TO him
jokes.explanation: The phrasing 'a little thing called a subpoena' is doing excellent work — Hank's grandiosity married to his victimhood. The casual framing of litigation as inevitable is very Hank: litigious, self-righteous, and convinced of his own innocence. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Larry's closing rant: 'these people... they just think they can push us all around because, ooh, they're the network. The network people. Idiots.'
jokes.setup: Larry wraps up the on-air segment ostensibly resolving the network feud.
jokes.punchline: He immediately re-ignites the conflict with another on-air insult, calling them idiots — the apology was completely hollow.
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing irony: the 'apology' sequence ends with Larry calling the network idiots again on air. The 'Idiots.' kicker echoes his earlier monologue and is the episode's structural loop closing. Not a surprising joke, but satisfying as a character conclusion.

jokes.text: Larry's editorial during the post-show debrief: 'These people, if you don't mind my...they...they just think they can push us all around because, ooh, they're the network. Idiots.'
jokes.setup: Larry is complaining to Artie about the network's behavior
jokes.punchline: The 'ooh, they're the network' mini-impression, combined with 'Idiots' as the terminal judgment, is Larry at his most Larry — performative outrage covering real anxiety
jokes.explanation: The 'Idiots' button is a recurring Larry verbal tic in this episode, and this final deployment (after the apology has already happened) captures his complete inability to let anything go. The 'ooh, they're the NETWORK' sarcasm is a nice characterization of his contempt.

tmdb_overview: Larry gets into a feud with the network when he makes fun of their new fall schedule on the air.
